lesson.body_markdown:
## Labour, employment and entrepreneurship

**Labour** is the physical and mental effort people use to produce goods and services. The **labour force** is made up of people of working age who are employed or are actively looking for work. **Employment** can be **wage employment** (working for an employer) or **self-employment** (running your own business, such as a farmer, tailor or trader).

**Sectors.** The **formal sector** has registered businesses, written contracts and regular wages, for example banks and government offices. The **informal sector** has small, often unregistered activities such as roadside trading, kenkey selling and small repair shops. In Ghana most workers earn a living in the informal sector.

**Unemployment** means being without work while able and willing to work and actively seeking it. Types include **seasonal** (work available only in certain seasons, such as farming in the dry season), **frictional** (between jobs), **structural** (skills do not match available jobs) and **disguised** (more workers than needed, so some add nothing to output). The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.

The Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651) protects workers and sets a minimum age for employment.

**Entrepreneurship.** An **entrepreneur** organises land, labour and capital, and takes the risk of starting a business in order to make a profit. Profit = revenue minus total costs. Small businesses create jobs, use local materials and spread income, but often lack capital, record keeping and markets. Sources of capital include the owner's savings, family, loans from banks and microfinance firms, and supplier credit.
key_points: Wage employment means working for others; self-employment means running your own business.
Unemployment types include seasonal, frictional, structural and disguised.
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100.
An entrepreneur organises resources and takes risks to earn profit; profit = revenue - costs.
Small businesses create jobs but often lack capital and records.

Incorrect. An auditor checks financial records and does not start the business.
Correct. An entrepreneur combines resources and bears the risk of starting a business.

topics.title: Colonial Rule and the Independence Struggle

lesson.body_markdown:
## Colonial rule and the independence struggle

Before colonial rule, the area now called Ghana was home to many states such as Asante, Fante and Dagbon. Europeans came for trade in gold, ivory and later enslaved people. The Portuguese built Elmina Castle in 1482, and the area became known as the **Gold Coast** because of its gold. Britain later gained control of the coast and the interior.

**Steps in British control.** By the **Bond of 1844**, Fante chiefs accepted British influence in the settlement of serious crimes. In 1874 the coastal area became the Gold Coast Colony, and Accra replaced Cape Coast as capital in 1877. The Asante were defeated in several wars. In 1900 the Governor, Sir Frederick Hodgson, demanded the Golden Stool, which led to the War of the Golden Stool led by **Yaa Asantewaa**, Queen Mother of Ejisu.

**Colonial administration.** Britain used **indirect rule**, governing through existing chiefs under British officials. Governor Gordon Guggisberg (1919-1927) expanded roads, railways, the Korle Bu hospital and Achimota school.

**Resistance and nationalism.** The Aborigines' Rights Protection Society (1897) opposed laws that threatened land. The 1946 Burns Constitution gave Africans a majority of unofficial seats in the Legislative Council. After the 1948 disturbances, the Watson Commission was set up. In 1949 Kwame Nkrumah formed the Convention People's Party and in 1950 led the Positive Action campaign of strikes and non-cooperation. Independence came on 6 March 1957.

lesson.body_markdown:
## Information, media and communication

**Communication** is the sharing of information, ideas and feelings. **Mass media** are channels that reach large audiences at once: newspapers, radio, television and online platforms. Ghana has state-owned media, such as the Ghana Broadcasting Corporation, and many private radio and television stations and online news sites.

**Roles of the media.** The media **inform** the public, **educate** (health, farming and civic education), **entertain**, and act as a **watchdog** by exposing corruption and holding leaders accountable. They also provide a platform for public debate before and during elections.

**Constitutional guarantees.** Article 21 of the 1992 Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression, including freedom of the press and other media, and Article 21 also protects the right to information. Chapter 12 (Articles 162 to 164) guarantees the freedom and independence of the media: there is no censorship, no licence is required to set up a newspaper, and state-owned media must give fair opportunity to divergent views. These freedoms are not absolute; they are subject to laws needed to protect national security, public order, public morality and the reputations and rights of others. The National Media Commission, created under Article 166, helps to safeguard the independence of the media. The Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989) gives citizens access to information held by public institutions.

**Responsible use.** **Misinformation** is false information shared without intent to harm; **disinformation** is deliberately false. Before sharing a social media post, check the source, date and other reports, and avoid posting private or insulting material.
key_points: Media inform, educate, entertain and act as a watchdog.
Article 21 protects freedom of speech and expression; Articles 162-164 protect media freedom and independence.
Media freedom is limited by laws protecting security, order, morality and others' reputations.
The National Media Commission (Art. 166) safeguards media independence.
Check sources before sharing; disinformation is deliberately false.
